passages.title: Black Holes: Where Light Can't Escape
paragraphs: Imagine something so heavy and so tightly packed that nothing can escape its pull, not even light, the fastest thing in the universe. That is a black hole. Because no light comes out of it, a black hole looks completely black, which is how it got its name.

Most black holes form when a very large star runs out of fuel. Without the energy that pushed outward from its center, the star can no longer hold itself up. Its core collapses under its own gravity, squeezing an enormous amount of matter into a tiny space. Some black holes are several times heavier than our Sun, while the giant ones at the centers of galaxies are millions or even billions of times heavier.

The edge of a black hole is called the event horizon. Anything that crosses it, whether dust, gas or light, can never come back out. Scientists think that if an astronaut fell toward a small black hole, the pull on their feet would be so much stronger than the pull on their head that they would be stretched out like a noodle. Scientists even have a funny name for this: spaghettification.

If black holes are black, how do we find them? Scientists watch how they affect things nearby. Stars can be seen racing around an invisible object, and gas falling toward a black hole heats up and glows brightly before it disappears. In 2019, scientists using telescopes around the world shared the first picture of the glowing ring around a black hole in a galaxy called M87. In 2022, they shared a picture of Sagittarius A*, the black hole at the center of our own Milky Way galaxy.
Do not worry, though. The nearest black hole we know of is more than a thousand light-years away, far too distant to pull in our planet.

questions.prompt: Why does a black hole look completely black?
options: It is covered in space dust
Not even light can escape its pull
It is always on the dark side of a planet

questions.prompt: What is the edge of a black hole called?
What happens right after a very large star runs out of fuel?
options: Its core collapses under its own gravity

questions.prompt: Scientists cannot see a black hole directly. How do they find one?
options: By listening for loud noises in space
By watching how nearby stars and gas behave

questions.prompt: What is the name of the black hole at the center of the Milky Way?

passages.title: Andrés Bonifacio and the Katipunan

imageCredit.author: Chofre y Cia (now Cacho Hermanos Inc.)

paragraphs: Andrés Bonifacio was born on November 30, 1863, in Tondo, Manila. His family was not rich. When he was a teenager, both of his parents died, and he left school to take care of his younger brothers and sisters. To earn money, he made and sold canes and paper fans. Later, he worked as a clerk and messenger for companies in Manila.

Even though he stopped going to school, Bonifacio never stopped learning. He taught himself by reading many books, including the novels of José Rizal and books about the French Revolution. These books helped him see that Filipinos living under Spanish rule deserved freedom and fair treatment.

In 1892, José Rizal started a group called La Liga Filipina, which asked for peaceful changes. Only days later, Rizal was arrested and sent away to Dapitan. Bonifacio decided that asking politely was not enough. On July 7, 1892, he and his companions founded a secret society called the Katipunan. Its members promised to fight for the country's independence, and thousands of Filipinos joined.

In August 1896, the Spanish discovered the secret society. Bonifacio gathered the Katipuneros, and as a sign that they would no longer obey Spain, they tore up their cédulas, the tax certificates the Spanish government made people carry. This event is remembered as the Cry of Pugad Lawin, and it marked the start of the Philippine Revolution.

Bonifacio died in 1897 after a conflict among the leaders of the revolution, but the fight he started went on. Today he is honored as one of the country's national heroes, and every November 30, on his birthday, Filipinos celebrate Bonifacio Day.

passages.title: The Amazing Octopus
paragraphs: With eight wiggly arms, three hearts and blue blood, the octopus might sound like a creature from a science-fiction movie. But it is real, and it lives in oceans all around the world, from warm coral reefs to the cold, dark deep sea.

An octopus has no bones at all. Its only hard body part is its beak, shaped a little like a parrot's, which it uses to crack open crabs and clams. Because the rest of its body is soft, an octopus can squeeze through any gap bigger than its beak. Some octopuses kept in aquariums have even escaped from their tanks this way!

The octopus is also one of the smartest animals without a backbone. Scientists have watched octopuses solve puzzles, open jars to reach food and carry coconut shells to use as portable shelters. Surprisingly, about two-thirds of an octopus's nerve cells, called neurons, are in its arms instead of its head. Each arm can feel, and even taste, whatever its suckers touch.

When danger comes near, an octopus has plenty of tricks. Special cells in its skin, called chromatophores, let it change color in less than a second to blend in with rocks or coral. It can even make its skin look bumpy or smooth. If a predator still gets too close, the octopus squirts a cloud of dark ink and jets away.

Octopuses do not live very long. Many kinds live for only one or two years. A mother octopus guards her eggs for weeks or even months, often without eating, until her babies hatch and drift away into the sea.

questions.prompt: How many hearts does an octopus have?
Why can an octopus squeeze through tiny gaps?
options: Its body is soft, with only a hard beak

questions.prompt: What are the skin cells that let an octopus change color called?
Where are about two-thirds of an octopus's neurons?
What is this text mostly about?
options: The surprising body, brain and tricks of the octopus

passages.title: DNA: The Code Inside Every Cell
paragraphs: Why do you have your mother's smile or your grandfather's curly hair? Why does a mango seed grow into a mango tree and never into a coconut palm? The answer is hidden inside living cells, in a molecule called DNA.

Your body is made of trillions of tiny cells, and tucked inside most of them is DNA: a very long, very thin molecule shaped like a twisted ladder. Scientists call this shape a double helix. If you could unwind the DNA from just one of your cells and stretch it out, it would be about two meters long, yet it fits inside a space far smaller than the dot on a letter i.

DNA works like an instruction book written in a code with only four letters: A, T, C and G. The rungs of the twisted ladder are made of these four chemical bases, and they always pair the same way: A with T, and C with G. The order of the letters spells out instructions. A section of DNA that holds the instructions for one job, such as helping to give your eyes their color, is called a gene.

You get half of your DNA from your mother and half from your father. That is why children often look a little like both parents. All humans share about 99.9 percent of their DNA, so tiny differences are what make each person unique.

In the early 1950s, scientist Rosalind Franklin used X-rays to take a famous image of DNA, known as Photo 51. With the help of her work, James Watson and Francis Crick described the double helix in 1953. Today, understanding DNA helps doctors treat diseases, helps farmers grow stronger crops and even helps solve crimes.

options: They get half of their DNA from each parent

options: Watson and Crick described the double helix

passages.title: The Great Pyramid of Giza
paragraphs: On the edge of the desert near Cairo, Egypt, stands one of the oldest and most famous buildings on Earth: the Great Pyramid of Giza. It was built about 4,500 years ago as a tomb for a pharaoh, or king, named Khufu. It is the oldest of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and the only one still standing.

The Great Pyramid is enormous. It was built from about 2.3 million blocks of stone, and many of them weigh more than two tons each, about as much as a small car. When it was finished, it rose about 146 meters high. For nearly 4,000 years, it was the tallest structure people had ever built.

How did the ancient Egyptians build it without modern machines? Workers cut stone with copper tools and moved the heavy blocks on wooden sledges. Some blocks came from far away, carried along the Nile River by boat. Scientists have found that wetting the sand in front of a sledge makes it much easier to pull, and ramps of mud and stone probably helped raise the blocks higher and higher.

For a long time, many people believed that slaves built the pyramids. But archaeologists have discovered the villages where the builders lived, along with their bakeries and even their tombs. This evidence shows that the builders were skilled, paid workers who were proud of their work.

The ancient Egyptians believed that a pharaoh's spirit lived on after death. The pyramid protected Khufu's body and the treasures he would need in the afterlife. Even today, scientists are using new technology to discover hidden spaces inside the Great Pyramid.

passages.title: Artificial Intelligence: How Computers Learn
paragraphs: When you ask a voice assistant about the weather, get a movie suggestion on a video app or use a tool that translates English into Filipino, you are using artificial intelligence, or AI. AI is a kind of computer program that can do tasks that usually need human thinking, like recognizing pictures, understanding speech and answering questions.

Most computer programs follow exact rules written by programmers. Many AI systems work differently: they learn from examples. Imagine teaching a computer to recognize cats. Instead of describing every kind of cat, people show it thousands of photos labeled "cat" and "not a cat." The program searches for patterns, such as pointy ears and whiskers, and slowly gets better at telling them apart. Learning from lots of examples like this is called machine learning.
AI can be incredibly helpful. It helps doctors spot signs of disease in medical scans, helps farmers check the health of their crops and helps scientists study huge amounts of information quickly.

But AI also makes mistakes. It only knows what it has learned from its examples, and if those examples are incomplete or unfair, the AI can give wrong or unfair answers. An AI tool can even sound very sure of itself while saying something that is not true. That is why people must always check important information, and why the people who build AI need to test it carefully.

Here are some smart habits for using AI tools: never share private information like your address or passwords, ask a trusted adult when you are unsure, and remember that AI is a helper for your thinking, not a replacement for it.

options: By showing it thousands of photos labeled cat and not a cat

options: It learned from examples that were incomplete or unfair

options: AI learns from examples and can be very helpful, but people must use it carefully
